analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and replaces it with age-based tax credits, expanded health savings accounts, and high-risk pool grants.
analysis.headline: A full repeal-and-replace bill with 85 Republican cosponsors never got a committee vote in two years and died when Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have erased the Affordable Care Act, ending its guaranteed-coverage rules, subsidies, and Medicaid expansion. In its place it offers refundable tax credits based on age to help buy insurance, much larger tax-advantaged health savings accounts, and federal grants to states for high-risk pools for people too sick to buy coverage cheaply. It would let insurers turn people away outside open enrollment and exclude preexisting conditions in some cases, and it gives doctors new legal protections, including an exemption from antitrust rules when negotiating with insurers.
analysis.who_benefits: People who buy their own insurance — especially younger and healthier ones — would get refundable tax credits ($900 to $3,000 per person per month depending on age) and expanded health savings accounts, and insurers would gain flexibility to price and deny coverage. Doctors would gain a shield from antitrust law when negotiating with insurers, protection in malpractice suits, and the right to bill Medicare patients privately.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People buying individual insurance, insurers, doctors

how_it_helps.text: Replaces ACA subsidies with refundable tax credits for buying health insurance, worth $900/month per child, $1,200/month for adults 18-34, $2,100 for 35-49, and $3,000 for 50 and up, adjusted for inflation [S3].
Lets people who get benefits from Medicare, Medicaid, TRICARE, veterans coverage, or employer plans opt out and take the tax credit instead [S3].

Raises health savings account contribution limits, adds a $1,000 refundable credit for HSA contributions, lets HSAs pay direct primary-care fees, and gives HSAs bankruptcy protection like retirement accounts [S2] [S3].
Authorizes $1 billion a year for three years in grants to states for high-risk or reinsurance pools to subsidize coverage for people with expensive health conditions [S2] [S3].

Exempts health care professionals from federal and state antitrust laws when negotiating with health plans, and lets Medicare beneficiaries privately contract with doctors and still submit claims to Medicare [S2].
Caps the tax-free employer health benefit at $8,000 for individual and $20,000 for family coverage, ending the unlimited tax break on the most generous plans [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: People with preexisting conditions and expensive health needs: with guaranteed issue and community rating repealed, insurers could deny coverage outside open enrollment and exclude preexisting conditions under certain conditions, leaving them dependent on state high-risk pools. Low- and middle-income households would lose income-scaled ACA subsidies and Medicaid expansion in favor of flat age-based credits that may not cover their premiums. Patients injured by malpractice would face new limits under clinical-guideline rules.
analysis.who_pays_short: People with preexisting conditions, low-income households

drawbacks.text: Insurers offering individual coverage could deny coverage to an individual outside open enrollment periods, and preexisting conditions could be excluded from coverage under certain conditions [S2].

The bill bars any mandate for guaranteed issue or community rating in the private insurance market, removing the ACA's core protection that everyone can buy coverage at standard rates regardless of health [S3].

The tax credits are flat amounts based on age, not income, so a household earning $30,000 and one earning $300,000 get the same credit; the credits also cannot be used for any plan covering abortion, with narrow exceptions [S3].
The bill caps the employer health coverage tax exclusion at $8,000 individual and $20,000 family, which would raise taxes on employees with more expensive employer plans [S3].
In health care lawsuits, compliance with federal clinical practice guidelines would change the burden of proof, making it harder for injured patients to prevail [S2].
The $1 billion-a-year high-risk pool funding is a fixed appropriation; similar state pools historically struggled to cover everyone who needed them once insurers could screen out sick applicants.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers real help to some people: refundable credits for anyone buying insurance, bigger and more flexible health savings accounts, and high-risk pool funding for those priced out. But the design shifts the largest burdens onto the people least able to bear them — those with preexisting conditions, who lose the guarantee of affordable coverage and depend on a fixed $3 billion pool, and lower-income households, who trade income-scaled subsidies for flat credits. Generous protections for doctors (antitrust exemption, malpractice shields) and freedom for insurers to pick which state's rules govern their plans add costs and uncertainty without a matching benefit for patients. It is a coherent conservative redesign, but the trade-offs run against older, sicker, and poorer households.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in nine House committees and their subcommittees for nearly two years; no committee ever voted on it, no floor vote ever happened, and it expired when that Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom Price (R-GA) introduced the bill on May 13, 2015, with 84 Republican cosponsors joining [S1] [S4].

It was referred to nine House committees at once — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, Judiciary, Natural Resources, House Administration, Rules, Appropriations, and Oversight and Government Reform [S5].
Within weeks it was sent to subcommittees, including the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee and the Ways and Means Health Subcommittee, where it remained [S5].
No committee held a markup, no vote was ever scheduled, and the last recorded action was a subcommittee referral on November 16, 2015 [S5].
The 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, and the bill died with it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People with preexisting conditions and ACA marketplace enrollees kept the law's guaranteed-coverage protections and subsidies, and insurers kept a guaranteed-issue individual market with subsidized customers — the replacement plan never became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People with preexisting conditions; insurers kept the ACA market

sides.party_line_note: All 85 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, and the House's Republican majority never advanced the bill to a vote; no Democrat supported it.

industries.note: The bill ends the ACA's subsidized exchange market but hands insurers freedom to deny coverage outside open enrollment, exclude preexisting conditions in some cases, and pick which state's rules govern their individual plans. The freed-up pricing power comes largely at sick and older customers' expense, while high-risk pool grants subsidize the coverage states must otherwise provide.

Doctors get an exemption from antitrust laws when negotiating with health plans, the right to privately contract with Medicare patients and still bill Medicare, and a malpractice regime where following federal clinical guidelines shifts the burden of proof. Some provisions could raise patient costs or make it harder for injured patients to win lawsuits.
The bill raises HSA limits, adds a $1,000 refundable contribution credit, and routes any excess insurance credit into HSAs, expanding the accounts banks and trustees manage.
Ministry membership is treated as qualifying coverage, letting members establish HSAs and count toward the tax credit.
